rationale:
The supplied proof combines two separate mathematical obligations, and both are reusable on their own.
(B) Step 1, localization. A measure that is finite on compact subsets of an open U is "open σ-finite" on U in the sense of Simon Ch. 1 Def. 1.14: U is the union of countably many open sets W_i with μ(W_i) < ∞. This is pure topology/measure bookkeeping. The sibling boundary_measurable node has identical hypotheses and needs the same fact.
(A) Steps 2–3. The Lebesgue–Besicovitch differentiation theorem along OPEN balls for a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N: normalAverage μ f x ρ → f(x) for μ-a.e. x, for any f ∈ L¹(μ). Simon Ch. 1 Cor. 3.17 and Mathlib's Besicovitch Vitali family use closed balls, while the Ch. 3 contract's normalAverage (4.2) uses open balls. So A's real content is the closed-to-open passage, including the μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 case, on top of the Mathlib differentiation theorem. This is exactly the result Simon invokes at chapter-03.txt line 584.

I did not make the closed-ball step its own child: in this Mathlib it is a 4-line corollary (VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average composed with Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt, rewritten with setAverage_eq and measureReal_def), so it stays inside A.

How the children give the parent (parent Step 4; compiled in Lean):
1. Take W_i from B.
2. μ_i := μ.restrict W_i is finite.
3. ν ∈ L¹(μ_i) by Integrable.of_bound, using hν.restrict and ‖ν‖ ≤ 1 μ_i-a.e.
4. A gives ∀ᵐ x ∂μ_i, normalAverage μ_i ν x → ν x. Since W_i is open, hence measurable, ae_restrict_iff' turns this into ∀ᵐ x ∂μ, x ∈ W_i → ….
5. Combine over i ∈ ℕ with ae_all_iff, then add x ∈ U a.e. (from μ Uᶜ = 0) and ‖ν x‖ = 1 a.e.
6. For such an x, pick i with x ∈ W_i and R > 0 with B_R(x) ⊆ W_i. For ρ ∈ (0, R), μ_i(B_ρ(x)) = μ(B_ρ(x)) and ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ν dμ_i = ∫_{B_ρ(x)} ν dμ (restrict_apply, restrict_restrict). So normalAverage μ ν x → ν x with ‖ν x‖ = 1 and x ∈ U, i.e. x ∈ reducedBoundary U μ ν.
7. Hence μ (reducedBoundary U μ ν)ᶜ = 0 by measure_eq_zero_iff_ae_notMem. This works for the outer measure, so the reduced boundary need not be measurable.

subproblems.title: Lebesgue–Besicovitch differentiation along open balls for a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N (normalAverage μ f x → f(x) μ-a.e.)
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let μ be a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) (μ(ℝ^N) < ∞), and let f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N be μ-integrable. Then for μ-almost every x ∈ ℝ^N, normalAverage μ f x ρ := μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal⁻¹ • ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ converges to f(x) as ρ ↓ 0. Here B_ρ(x) is the open ball, t.toReal is the real value of t ∈ [0, ∞], and 0⁻¹ = 0, so the average is 0 when μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Rn N)) (f : Rn N → Rn N), IsFiniteMeasure μ → Integrable f μ → ∀ᵐ x ∂μ, Tendsto (normalAverage μ f x) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (f x))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Steps 2–3 of the parent proof.
- The differentiation result is Simon Ch. 1, Corollary 3.17 (Lebesgue differentiation theorem; chapter-01.txt lines 927–969).
- It applies to every Radon measure on ℝ^N, because such measures have the Symmetric Vitali Property (Remark 3.11(3), via the Besicovitch Covering Lemma 3.12; chapter-01.txt lines 800–850).
- This is the result Simon Ch. 3 invokes at chapter-03.txt line 584 ("by virtue of Theorem 3.23 of Ch. 1 we have μ_E(U ∖ ∂*E) = 0").
- Simon's Ch. 1 balls B_ρ(x) are closed: line 591 reserves a separate symbol for open balls. In contrast, normalAverage and the reduced boundary (Ch. 3 (4.2), contract) use open balls. Steps 2–4 below carry out the parent's closed-to-open passage.
- Mathlib: Besicovitch.vitaliFamily, VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average, Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt, setAverage_eq, measureReal_def, tendsto_measure_iUnion_atTop, tendsto_setIntegral_of_monotone.

Notation.
- B_r(x) is the open ball and B̄_r(x) the closed ball.
- For a Borel set A ⊆ ℝ^N, avg(A) := μ(A).toReal⁻¹ • ∫_A f dμ. Here t.toReal ∈ [0, ∞) is the real value of t ∈ [0, ∞] (with ∞.toReal = 0), and 0⁻¹ := 0.
- Thus normalAverage μ f x ρ = avg(B_ρ(x)). Put c_x(r) := avg(B̄_r(x)).
- If μ(A) = 0 then avg(A) = 0⁻¹ • ∫_A f dμ = 0.

1. Lebesgue–Besicovitch differentiation along closed balls.
   - ℝ^N = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) is a finite-dimensional normed space. Hence it is a second-countable metric space with the Borel σ-algebra and has the Besicovitch covering property.
   - μ is finite, hence s-finite and locally finite. f ∈ L¹(μ) is locally integrable.
   - Therefore the closed balls {B̄_r(x) : r > 0} form a Vitali family for μ (Besicovitch.vitaliFamily μ).
   - The Lebesgue differentiation theorem for Vitali families (VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average) gives a μ-null set Z such that, for every x ∉ Z, the averages avg(a) = ⨍_a f dμ converge to f(x) as a shrinks to x along this family.
   - As r ↓ 0, B̄_r(x) shrinks to x along the family (Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt). So for every x ∉ Z, c_x(r) → f(x) as r ↓ 0.
   - Fix x ∉ Z. Steps 2–5 are deterministic.

2. Let ε > 0. By Step 1, choose δ > 0 such that ‖c_x(r) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2 for all r ∈ (0, δ). Fix ρ ∈ (0, δ). Steps 3–4 show that ‖avg(B_ρ(x)) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2.

3. Case μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0.
   - Then avg(B_ρ(x)) = 0.
   - Since B̄_{ρ/2}(x) ⊆ B_ρ(x), also μ(B̄_{ρ/2}(x)) = 0, so c_x(ρ/2) = 0.
   - As ρ/2 ∈ (0, δ), ‖avg(B_ρ(x)) − f(x)‖ = ‖0 − f(x)‖ = ‖c_x(ρ/2) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2.

4. Case μ(B_ρ(x)) > 0.
   For n ∈ ℕ put r_n := ρ − ρ/(n + 2).
   - Since n + 2 ≥ 2, ρ/2 ≤ r_n < ρ.
   - (r_n) is nondecreasing. So (B̄_{r_n}(x))_n is a nondecreasing sequence of closed (hence Borel) sets, each contained in B_ρ(x).
   - Its union is B_ρ(x). Indeed, if |y − x| < ρ, choose n ∈ ℕ with n > ρ/(ρ − |y − x|). Then n + 2 > ρ/(ρ − |y − x|), so ρ/(n + 2) < ρ − |y − x|, i.e. |y − x| < r_n.
   (a) Measures. By continuity of measure from below, μ(B̄_{r_n}(x)) → μ(B_ρ(x)) in [0, ∞].
       - Since μ is finite, μ(B_ρ(x)) ∈ (0, ∞).
       - toReal is continuous at finite values, so μ(B̄_{r_n}(x)).toReal → μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal ≠ 0.
       - t ↦ t⁻¹ is continuous at every t ≠ 0, so μ(B̄_{r_n}(x)).toReal⁻¹ → μ(B_ρ(x)).toReal⁻¹.
   (b) Integrals. f is μ-integrable on B_ρ(x) = ⋃_n B̄_{r_n}(x). The functions 1_{B̄_{r_n}(x)} f converge pointwise to 1_{B_ρ(x)} f and are dominated by |f| ∈ L¹(μ). By dominated convergence, ∫_{B̄_{r_n}(x)} f dμ → ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ.
   (c) Passing to the limit.
       - Scalar multiplication ℝ × ℝ^N → ℝ^N is continuous, so by (a) and (b), c_x(r_n) → avg(B_ρ(x)) as n → ∞.
       - Every r_n lies in (0, δ), since 0 < ρ/2 ≤ r_n < ρ < δ. Hence ‖c_x(r_n) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2 for all n.
       - The set {w : ‖w − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2} is closed, so it contains the limit: ‖avg(B_ρ(x)) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2.

5. Conclusion. By Steps 2–4, for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with ‖normalAverage μ f x ρ − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2 < ε for all ρ ∈ (0, δ). That is, normalAverage μ f x ρ → f(x) as ρ ↓ 0: Tendsto (normalAverage μ f x) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (f x)). This holds for every x outside the μ-null set Z, which is the claim (∀ᵐ x ∂μ). ∎
proof_key_steps: Lebesgue–Besicovitch differentiation (VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average for Besicovitch.vitaliFamily μ, composed with Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt): for μ-a.e. x, the closed-ball averages c_x(r) = μ(B̄_r(x)).toReal⁻¹ • ∫_{B̄_r(x)} f dμ tend to f(x) as r ↓ 0.
Fix such an x and ε > 0; choose δ with ‖c_x(r) − f(x)‖ ≤ ε/2 on (0, δ); fix ρ ∈ (0, δ).
If μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0, the open-ball average and c_x(ρ/2) both vanish, so the bound transfers.

If μ(B_ρ(x)) > 0, the closed balls of radii r_n = ρ − ρ/(n+2) increase to B_ρ(x). Continuity from below, toReal/inverse continuity and dominated convergence give c_x(r_n) → normalAverage μ f x ρ, and the closed bound ≤ ε/2 passes to the limit.
Hence Tendsto (normalAverage μ f x) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (f x)) for μ-a.e. x.

subproblems.title: Exhaustion of an open U ⊆ ℝ^N by countably many open sets of finite μ-measure (μ finite on compact subsets of U)
subproblems.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let U ⊆ ℝ^N be open, and let μ be a (Borel) measure on ℝ^N with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U. Then there are open sets W_0, W_1, W_2, … ⊆ ℝ^N such that μ(W_i) < ∞ for every i ∈ ℕ and ⋃_{i ∈ ℕ} W_i = U.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (U : Set (Rn N)) (μ : Measure (Rn N)), IsOpen U → (∀ K : Set (Rn N), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → μ K < ∞) → ∃ W : ℕ → Set (Rn N), (∀ i, IsOpen (W i)) ∧ (∀ i, μ (W i) < ∞) ∧ ⋃ i, W i = U
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source.
- Step 1 (localization) of the parent proof, re-indexed by i ∈ ℕ: our W_i is the parent's W_{i+1}.
- Simon Ch. 1, Definition 1.14 ("open σ-finite": X = ⋃_j V_j with V_j open and μ(V_j) < ∞; chapter-01.txt lines 268–272) and the remark following it, as used in the proof of Ch. 1, Theorem 3.16 ("Since X = ∪_j V_j with V_j open and μ(V_j) < ∞ …").
- Mathlib: Metric.infEDist, Metric.continuous_infEDist, Metric.infEDist_zero_of_mem, Metric.mem_closure_iff_infEDist_zero, isCompact_closedBall, ENNReal.exists_inv_nat_lt, ENNReal.inv_le_inv.

Notation. For y ∈ ℝ^N and S ⊆ ℝ^N, let d(y, S) := inf_{z ∈ S} |y − z| ∈ [0, ∞]; so d(y, ∅) = ∞. Two standard facts are used:
(i) y ↦ d(y, S) is a continuous map ℝ^N → [0, ∞] (it is 1-Lipschitz);
(ii) d(y, S) = 0 iff y ∈ closure(S); in particular d(y, S) = 0 for y ∈ S.

1. Definitions. For i ∈ ℕ let c_i := (i + 1)⁻¹ ∈ [0, ∞]; c_i > 0 because i + 1 ≠ ∞. Define
   W_i := B_{i+1}(0) ∩ {y : c_i < d(y, Uᶜ)},
   K_i := B̄_{i+1}(0) ∩ {y : c_i ≤ d(y, Uᶜ)}.

2. If c_i ≤ d(y, Uᶜ), then y ∈ U. Otherwise y ∈ Uᶜ, so d(y, Uᶜ) = 0 by (ii), whence c_i ≤ 0, contradicting c_i > 0.

3. W_i is open.
   - B_{i+1}(0) is open.
   - {y : c_i < d(y, Uᶜ)} is the preimage of the open set (c_i, ∞] under the continuous map y ↦ d(y, Uᶜ), by (i).
   - An intersection of two open sets is open.

4. μ(W_i) < ∞.
   - The closed ball B̄_{i+1}(0) is compact (Heine–Borel; ℝ^N is a proper space).
   - {y : c_i ≤ d(y, Uᶜ)} is closed, being the preimage of the closed set [c_i, ∞] under a continuous map. So K_i, a closed subset of a compact set, is compact.
   - By Step 2, K_i ⊆ U.
   - B_{i+1}(0) ⊆ B̄_{i+1}(0), and c_i < d(y, Uᶜ) implies c_i ≤ d(y, Uᶜ). So W_i ⊆ K_i.
   - By monotonicity of μ and the hypothesis on compact subsets of U, μ(W_i) ≤ μ(K_i) < ∞.

5. ⋃_i W_i ⊆ U: every y ∈ W_i satisfies c_i ≤ d(y, Uᶜ), so y ∈ U by Step 2.

6. U ⊆ ⋃_i W_i. Let y ∈ U.
   - U is open, so Uᶜ is closed and closure(Uᶜ) = Uᶜ, which does not contain y. By (ii), d(y, Uᶜ) ≠ 0.
   - Since n⁻¹ → 0 in [0, ∞], there is n ∈ ℕ with n⁻¹ < d(y, Uᶜ) (ENNReal.exists_inv_nat_lt).
   - Choose m ∈ ℕ with m > |y| (Archimedean property) and set i := max(n, m).
   - Then |y| < m ≤ i < i + 1, so y ∈ B_{i+1}(0).
   - Also n ≤ i ≤ i + 1, and inversion is antitone on [0, ∞], so c_i = (i + 1)⁻¹ ≤ n⁻¹ < d(y, Uᶜ).
   - Hence y ∈ W_i.

7. By Steps 3–6, the W_i (i ∈ ℕ) are open sets with μ(W_i) < ∞ and ⋃_i W_i = U, which is the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: Define W_i = B_{i+1}(0) ∩ {y : d(y, Uᶜ) > (i+1)⁻¹} and K_i = B̄_{i+1}(0) ∩ {y : d(y, Uᶜ) ≥ (i+1)⁻¹}, with d the extended distance to Uᶜ.
d(y, Uᶜ) ≥ (i+1)⁻¹ > 0 forces y ∈ U, so K_i ⊆ U.
W_i is open (continuity of d(·, Uᶜ)), K_i is compact (closed and bounded), and W_i ⊆ K_i, so μ(W_i) ≤ μ(K_i) < ∞.
Every y ∈ U has d(y, Uᶜ) > 0 because Uᶜ is closed, so y ∈ W_i for i = max(n, m) with n⁻¹ < d(y, Uᶜ) and m > |y|. Hence ⋃_i W_i = U.
